title: HST image of hot blue stars at the core of M15
caption: Hot blue stars at the core of globular cluster M15, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 15, Messier 15, NGC 7078 · constellation Pegasus · about 35000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: G. De Marchi (STScI and Univ. of Florence, Italy) and F. Paresce (STScI)/NASA, ESA.

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: This Hubble image looks into the center of the globular cluster M15. In it, astronomers found about 15 very hot stars not seen before, sitting isolated at the cluster's core.

A globular cluster is a dense ball of stars held together by gravity, and its core is the most crowded part of all. That crowding may account for these unusual stars. The most likely explanation is that they are 'naked cores', stars that have been stripped of their outer envelopes of gas, exposing the hot interiors underneath.

For that to happen, the stars in the cluster's core must be so tightly packed that they can pull material off one another through gravity. Finding these stars therefore says something about conditions at the heart of M15, where stars crowd together closely enough to interfere with one another directly. That is very different from the Sun's surroundings, where neighboring stars are far apart.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (0.19 x 0.16 arcminutes) and distance (35000 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.9 × 1.6 light-years. Its light set out about 35,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the Hubble Space Telescope. The instrument, filters and color mapping are not published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view helps separate individual stars in the crowded core.
